gaps: The CText Shuowen page returned 403; its search result was not treated as inspected content. The Ministry of Education dictionary and CUHK database provide directly inspected corroboration of the Shuowen text.

Although CUHK indexes oracle-bone and bronze forms of 聽 and gives transcribed examples, glyph images were not visually inspected here. Exact earliest archaeological attestation and dating of each graphic variant remain unverified.

The evidence supports 口 as the semantic category for the old smiling sense and received Shuowen’s 斤-as-phonetic analysis. The local Baxter–Sagart table supplied here contains no row for 斤 or the older 听 word, so no same-system Baxter–Sagart component/host comparison can be reported. Zhengzhang reconstructions are separately identified and cannot fill that missing Baxter–Sagart comparison.

The specific account that an intermediate 𠯸 with 厅 phonetic was copied and corrupted/assimilated into 听 is reported by Wiktionary but not independently demonstrated from inspected primary manuscript evidence. Its precise chronology and mechanism remain unresolved.

The separate histories of the 听 ‘smiling’ word and 聽 ‘hear/listen’ are established in the dictionaries, but the exact date and textual path by which the former graph began representing the latter word is not established by the sources inspected. Song-Yuan vernacular use is reported by the Taiwan Ministry dictionary.

No local row for a possible sound component 厅 was supplied, and no ancient pronunciation/name for the hall-related graph was independently recovered. The proposed 厅 phonetic intermediary therefore remains a graphic-analysis claim, not an independently verified sound reconstruction.

The Ministry dictionary quotes the Han Shanglin fu example and a Tang example for 听 ‘smiling’; it does not establish when this sense first arose. The academic article’s accessible abstract lists classical examples for hearing-related meanings but does not give a complete dated semantic chronology.
No reuse-license verification was performed for the repeatedly encountered online sources, so no tracked text extract is recommended.
No primary artifact image for the old 听 ‘smiling’ graph was established. The selected glyph candidate depicts 聽 in Shuowen seal style and is a modern redraw, not an artifact photograph.

The Ministry dictionary dates a Han literary example for ‘smiling’ and cites a Tang example, but these are textual attestations, not evidence for the graph’s earliest archaeological form. The exact first attestation remains unestablished.

The old 听 ‘smiling’ sense and 听 as a form of 聽 are separately supported, but the date and textual path by which the graph began representing ‘hear/listen’ remain uncertain. The proposed intermediate 𠯸 with 厅 phonetic and its alleged graphic corruption into 听 were not independently verified from primary manuscript evidence in this pass.

The received 斤 phonetic analysis is attested in Shuowen; comparative Old Chinese pronunciations here come from a secondary Zhengzhang transcription. No local Baxter–Sagart rows for 听 in its older sense or 斤 were supplied, so a same-system Baxter–Sagart comparison is unavailable. Supplied Baxter–Sagart 聽 readings belong to the 聽 lexical record, not to the old smiling-word/component comparison.

No direct character-specific Xiaoxuetang image or official rights notice was verified during this pass. The Sinica release notice inspected concerns the distinct component-search system and licenses different assets; it is not treated as permission for Xiaoxuetang images.
No reusable primary glyph for old 听 was verified. One supported, rights-documented image candidate for 聽 is proposed; its stylized image content was not visually inspected during this research stage.

The exact first attestation of the old 听 ‘smiling’ word and the chronology of its later use for 聽 remain unresolved; Han and Tang literary examples are reported in the supplied dossier, while Song-Yuan vernacular use is supported by the inspected Ministry record.

The 𠯸 → 听 corruption proposal and 厅 phonetic intermediary were not verified from inspected primary manuscript evidence. The proposed sound relationship has no independently checked historical readings for 厅 and 聽 in one reconstruction system.
The official Unihan records for 听 and 聽 returned internal errors in this pass. Provided local kMandarin rows are tīng for both, but current readings do not establish ancient phonetic relations.
No local Baxter–Sagart rows were supplied for 斤 or 听’s old ‘smiling’ sense; the checked Zhengzhang transcriptions must not be merged with Baxter–Sagart notation.

The selected Commons image is a modern seal-style redraw, not an artifact photo. Its description page was inspected, but the direct-image fetch returned a cache miss. The unavailable prior candidate 聽-seal.svg was not reused.
No tracked text extract is recommended: no exact-material reuse terms were verified for the repeatedly encountered dictionary texts.

The inspected sources establish Song-Yuan vernacular use of 听 for 聽, but do not establish when this use began or a borrowing mechanism based on sound similarity. The reviewed secondary proposal involving 𠯸 and phonetic 厅 was not verified against primary manuscript evidence.
The old 听 word’s Han and Tang literary examples document the smiling sense, but its earliest occurrence remains unknown.

The consulted primary dictionary record confirms Song–Yuan vernacular use of 听 for 聽, but does not establish that the words were borrowed because they sounded alike. The secondary 𠯸 plus 厅 explanation remains a proposed graphic/phonetic account; its asserted sound match, intermediate form, copying mechanism, and chronology were not independently verified from primary manuscript evidence.
The beginning date and textual path for 听 representing the “hear/listen” word remain unresolved; Song–Yuan vernacular use is the dated evidence inspected here.

The official Unihan character-record requests returned internal errors. Local supplied kMandarin readings are 听 tīng and 聽 tīng, but current readings do not prove ancient sound similarity or a borrowing mechanism.

The exact Commons page and its reuse terms were inspected, but opening its direct image URL returned an internal error. The page identifies a usable modern redraw candidate; image retrieval was not independently confirmed in this pass.
No separate reconstruction rows for 听’s older smiling word and 厅 were supplied. Baxter–Sagart rows for 聽 cannot establish a historical sound match for that distinct word and proposed component.

The Commons SVG page labels the file as 听 and cites a Sinica image record; direct SVG content could not be rendered in the web tool. The source record and the Ministry character entry corroborate the intended identity and association with the old smiling-word entry, but this pass does not independently compare pixel-level SVG content with Sinica’s original image.

The evidence supports describing the selected glyph as a modern Shuowen seal-style rendering associated with the older 听 entry and its received 口 + 斤 analysis. It does not support identifying it as an excavated artifact or as a 聽 glyph.
The age of the depicted small-seal form is an association with the received Shuowen tradition; this research did not inspect an artifact establishing the form’s archaeological date.

The Commons description and the character-specific Xiaoxuetang record both identify a 听 small-seal form, but the web tool could not retrieve the direct SVG or linked raster image bytes (cache misses); no independent pixel-level comparison is claimed.

The image is a modern digital redraw / query-interface rendering in Shuowen small-seal style, not a photograph of an ancient artifact. Its association with the Shuowen 口-section record does not establish an archaeological date.
The attached file is explicitly identified as 听, while the distinct 聽-seal.svg file is explicitly 聽. Neither modern redraw alone establishes the historical path by which 听 later represented 聽.
